cases.title: The starter about AI agents
cases.question: How does Brad ship with AI agents?
cases.answer:
Brad's essay describes a system where AI agents do most of the coding, with humans approving key steps. Brad runs VINDecoded, a profitable vehicle-research product on Android, iOS and the web, as a one-person engineering team where AI agents write most of the code. From June 13 to October 28, 2026, 1,235 pull requests merged into its monorepo, and 1,028 of them (83%) came from agent branches in Claude Code and Codex.

Agents work in isolation: every task gets its own git worktree: a separate checkout on its own branch. For medium and high-risk changes, the agent writes acceptance criteria as checkable lines, each naming its proof. When the code is done, a second agent reviews it with fresh context and only read tools, so it can't quietly fix what it finds. Production changes are gated: merging to master deploys nothing. Most new features reach production turned off, so merging and deploying code doesn't change what customers see.

cases.title: From the essay: features ship dark
cases.question: In Brad’s essay, how do new features reach customers?
cases.answer: New features reach customers through a staged process, and most ship turned off. Most new features reach production turned off, so merging and deploying code doesn't change what customers see. Turning it on is a separate, deliberate step that takes effect in seconds and can be undone the same way. The steps are: Merged dark. The code ships behind a gate that is off for everyone. Next, on for my account. I switch it on for myself in production through a per-user override. Then on for everyone. One command through the production-task CLI turns the gate on, for example `prod-task shop-ai:on`. Finally, Kept with a kill switch. Every live feature keeps a named off switch, such as `prod-task shop-ai:off`, and AGENTS.md lists it beside the feature.
